text: On the fifth of August, twenty twenty-one, FC Barcelona published a short statement. Lionel Messi would not be staying at the club.
He had agreed new terms. He had accepted a huge pay cut. Everyone expected him to sign. And then, at the last moment, it was over.
Three days later, he cried at a press conference in the Camp Nou. Two days after that, he was a Paris Saint-Germain player.
So what if the deal had gone through? What if Messi had stayed? In this video, we're going to build three honest scenarios — and see where each one takes Barça.
First, why he actually left — because the real reason is not the one most people remember.
Then three scenarios: a best case, a worst case, and the one we think is most likely. Everything that's a guess will be labelled as a model.
And at the end, a twist. Because some of the best things that have happened to Barça since may only have happened because he left.
Part one. Why he left.
Rewind one year. In August twenty twenty, after the eight–two defeat to Bayern Munich, Messi sent the club a formal request to leave. The club refused, and he stayed for one more season, unhappy.
In March twenty twenty-one, Joan Laporta was elected president. He was the president of the Ronaldinho years, a friend of Messi's, and he had promised to keep him.
At the end of June, Messi's contract ran out. For the first time in his adult life, he was technically a free agent.
Through July, the two sides agreed a new five-year deal, with Messi taking a reported fifty per cent pay cut. All that was left was to register the contract with La Liga.
That was the problem. La Liga has a spending limit for every club, based on its income. And Barça's finances were in ruins.

At his press conference, the new president explained it in one number. Without Messi, wages already took ninety-five per cent of the club's income. With Messi's new contract, even at half price, it would be one hundred and ten per cent.
Under the league's rules, there was simply no room to register a new contract for Messi — even at half the price.
There was one possible way out. La Liga was negotiating a deal with an investment fund, CVC, that would have given clubs a cash injection in exchange for a share of future TV money.
That cash might have made room for Messi. But Laporta decided the deal would mortgage the club's future for half a century. Barça refused to sign it.

So here is the first important thing. Messi didn't leave because he wanted to, or because Barça didn't want him. He left because of a decision about money — and a set of rules that the club had been breaking for years.
Part two. The ground rules.
Before we build scenarios, let's set the rules, so this is a fair game. The president stays the same. Ronald Koeman starts the season as coach, and Xavi arrives in November, like he did in real life.
Messi signs the deal he had agreed — five years, half his old salary.
And here's the rule most what-if videos skip. The money has to come from somewhere. To keep Messi, Barça either sign the CVC deal or cut even deeper somewhere else.
Finally, we're not going to pretend to know exact goals or points. Real statistics will appear in white. Anything we estimate will be labelled as a model.
First, let's remember what kind of player Barça would have been keeping. Messi was thirty-four, but he was not in decline in any normal sense.
In his last season at the club, he scored thirty goals in La Liga and finished as the league's top scorer — for the fifth season in a row.
He also won the Copa del Rey that year, scoring twice in the final. A month later, he won the Copa América with Argentina. He was still one of the best players on the planet.
Scenario one. The dream.
In the best case, Barça sign the CVC deal. The money arrives, Messi is registered, and nobody else important has to be sold.

Think about what that team would look like. Messi alongside a teenage Pedri, a seventeen-year-old Gavi breaking through, Frenkie de Jong, and Ansu Fati — the boy who had just inherited his number ten in real life.
With Xavi as coach from November, Messi becomes something like a playmaking forward — fewer sprints, more passes, still deciding big games.

Here's what actually happened that season. Barça finished second in the league, thirteen points behind Real Madrid. They went out of the Champions League in the group stage, for the first time in more than twenty years. And they were knocked out of the Europa League by Eintracht Frankfurt.
In the best-case model, a team with Messi probably gets out of that Champions League group. The margins were small, and a player who decides tight games changes small margins.
A title race with Madrid becomes possible. And in this version, Messi's farewell — whenever it came — happens on the pitch at the Camp Nou, in front of the fans, not in a press room.
Scenario two. The nightmare.
Now the opposite. In the worst case, Barça still refuse the CVC deal, and make room for Messi's salary by cutting even deeper.
That means selling players — and the players with the highest value were exactly the young ones the club's future depended on.
Imagine a version where one of Pedri, de Jong, or Araújo is sold to balance the books, so that a thirty-four-year-old can stay.
In this world, Barça keep the greatest player in their history — and lose a piece of the next generation.
There is also no room the following summer for new signings. In real life, in twenty twenty-two, Barça signed Robert Lewandowski and Raphinha. In this scenario, that's much harder.
And the club stays exactly where it had been since twenty seventeen: a team built around one brilliant, ageing player, waiting for him to save every big night.
Scenario three. The likely one.
The truth is usually somewhere in the middle. So here's the version we think is most likely.
Barça find just enough money — a little from the CVC deal or a similar one, a little from selling fringe players. Messi stays.
The first season is better than the real one, but not transformative. The team is still in transition, and the coach still changes in November.
By the second season, the club has the same problem as before: an expensive squad and a superstar heading towards his late thirties.
And there's a fascinating question in the middle of this path.

In December twenty twenty-two, Messi won the World Cup with Argentina. In real life, he did it as a PSG player, rested and focused. Would he have arrived in Qatar in the same condition after eighteen months as Barça's saviour? Nobody can know.
In the real twenty twenty-two, twenty-three season, Xavi's Barça won La Liga. In our likely scenario, they probably still do — this time with Messi.
And in the summer of twenty twenty-three, he says goodbye properly. A full Camp Nou, a lap of honour, a farewell that the real story never gave him.
Part three. What really happened.

Messi spent two seasons at Paris Saint-Germain. He won two French league titles, and scored thirty-two goals in seventy-five games. Good numbers for most players — but not the Messi Barcelona had known.
He never seemed truly at home there. And in twenty twenty-three, when his contract ended, there was talk of a return to Barcelona.
Once again, it was the club's finances that made it impossible. Messi chose Inter Miami instead.
Part four. The twist.
Here's the uncomfortable thought. When Messi left, the team had to find a new centre. Pedri and Gavi became that centre.
Because there was no money to buy stars, Barça turned back to their academy. Alejandro Balde. Fermín López. Pau Cubarsí. And a boy who was thirteen when Messi left — Lamine Yamal.
Would all of them have got their chance in a team built around Messi? Some would. But maybe not all of them, and maybe not so soon.
We'll never know which scenario was right. What we do know is that the way Messi left was a failure — of finances, of planning, and of a club that had lived beyond its means for years.
But the team that grew in the space he left behind is the most exciting Barça has had in a decade. Both of those things are true.
And Messi himself has said many times that Barcelona is his home. One day, in some role, many people expect to see him there again.
So which scenario do you believe? The dream, the nightmare, or the likely one? Tell me in the comments.
And if you want to understand the money that forced Messi out — and how Barça are climbing out of it — watch this next.
